name: Discontent and Grumbling

counsel.text: Discontent is a fretting humour, which dries the brains, wastes the spirits, corrodes and eats out the comfort of life; discontent makes a man that he doth not enjoy what he doth possess. A drop or two of vinegar will sour a whole glass of wine.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 8

counsel.text: These do secretly tax the wisdom of God, that he hath not screwed them up in their condition a peg higher.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 9

counsel.text: Learn quietly to submit to divine providence. Do not murmur at things that are ordered by divine wisdom. We may no more find fault with the works of providence than we may with the works of creation. It is a sin as much to quarrel with God's providence as to deny his providence.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: A Body of Divinity, the providence of God

counsel.text: Rise mightily against the first actings of thy distemper, its first conceptions; suffer it not to get the least ground. Do not say, "Thus far it shall go, and no farther." If it have allowance for one step, it will take another. It is impossible to fix bounds to sin.
counsel.author: John Owen
counsel.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 11

counsel.text: Get an humble spirit. The humble man is the contented man; if his estate be low, his heart is lower than his estate, therefore be content. If his esteem in the world be low, he that is little in his own eyes will not be much troubled to be little in the eyes of others.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 14

counsel.text: When the heart is once won to rest in God, to repose himself on him, he will assuredly satisfy it. He will never be as water that fails; nor hath he said at any time to the seed of Jacob, "Seek ye my face in vain." If Christ be chosen for the foundation of our supply, he will not fail us.
counsel.author: John Owen
counsel.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 14

counsel.text: Hath he not given thee himself to satisfy thee, his Son to save thee, his Spirit to lead thee, his grace to adorn thee, his covenant to assure thee, his mercy to pardon thee, his righteousness to clothe thee; and wilt thou murmur? Hath he not made thee a friend, a son, a brother, a bride, an heir; and wilt thou murmur?
counsel.author: Thomas Brooks
counsel.source: The Mute Christian Under the Smarting Rod

counsel.text: When he wills sickness, sickness is better than health; when he wills weakness, weakness is better than strength; when he wills want, want is better than wealth; when he wills reproach, reproach is better than honour; when he wills death, death is better than life. As God is wisdom itself, and so knows that which is best, so he is goodness itself, and therefore cannot do anything but that which is best: therefore hold thy peace.
counsel.author: Thomas Brooks
counsel.source: The Mute Christian Under the Smarting Rod

counsel.text: An humble heart thinks none less than himself, nor none worse than himself; an humble heart looks upon small mercies as great mercies, and great afflictions as small afflictions, and small afflictions as no afflictions; and therefore sits mute and quiet under all.
counsel.author: Thomas Brooks
counsel.source: The Mute Christian Under the Smarting Rod

counsel.text: Nothing should displease us that pleaseth God: neither should anything be pleasing to us that displeaseth him. This conformity is the ground of comfort.
counsel.author: Richard Sibbes
counsel.source: The Soul's Conflict with Itself, ch. 17

counsel.text: There is scarce any man, but the good he receives from God is more than the ill he feels, if our unthankful hearts would suffer us to think so. Is not our health more than our sickness? do we not enjoy more than we want, I mean, of the things that are necessary? are not our good days more than our evil? but we would go to heaven upon roses, and usually one cross is more taken to heart, than a hundred blessings. So unkindly we deal with God.
counsel.author: Richard Sibbes
counsel.source: The Soul's Conflict with Itself, ch. 10

counsel.text: If God cannot please thee, but thy heart riseth against him, what hopes are there of thy pleasing him, who will take nothing kindly from that man who is angry with him? And how can love to God be preserved in a discontented heart, that is always muttering against him?
counsel.author: William Gurnall

prayers.title: A prayer of confession
prayers.opening: Wise and sovereign Father, kind in all your ways, you work all things according to the counsel of your will, and the lines have fallen for me in the place you chose; I come to you in the name of your Son.
prayers.text: I confess that I have been discontented. I have grumbled about my circumstances as if you had made a mistake. I have complained in my heart and with my mouth, and I have forgotten your many mercies. Like Israel in the wilderness, I have murmured against you while you fed me every day. Underneath my complaining is a proud heart that thinks it deserves better, and an unbelieving heart that does not trust your goodness. This is ingratitude toward the kindest of fathers. Forgive me, Lord. Christ endured the cross for the joy set before him, and he learned obedience through what he suffered, without one murmur. For his sake pardon me. Holy Spirit, put this grumbling to death, and teach me, as you taught Paul, the secret of being content in plenty and in want.
prayers.closing: I thank you that your grace is sufficient for me, and that all things work together for good for those who love you. Blessed be your holy name, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

prayers.title: When I start to complain
prayers.opening: O Lord, you are good, and your steadfast love endures for ever.
prayers.text: Lord, I feel the complaint rising in me again. I bring it to you instead of letting it run. You have not wronged me. You are good, and your way is perfect even when I cannot understand it. Help me to count your mercies, beginning now, and to name them one by one. Teach me to say, The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. Lord Jesus, you had nowhere to lay your head, and you did not grumble. Holy Spirit, give me a thankful heart and a quiet mouth.
prayers.closing: Blessed be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and for evermore, through Jesus Christ. Amen.

prayers.title: For a thankful heart
prayers.opening: Bountiful Father, every good gift comes down from you, and your kindness to me is more than I can number.
prayers.text: Father, you have given me far more than I deserve: life and breath, daily bread, the gospel, your Son, your Spirit, and your church. Forgive me for passing over so much. Open my eyes to your daily kindness. Make me content with what I have, because you have said that you will never leave me nor forsake me. Teach me to give thanks in all circumstances, for this is your will for me in Christ Jesus. Let my mouth be full of your praise instead of complaint, so that others may see your goodness and come to trust you too.
prayers.closing: Through Jesus Christ, your greatest gift, to whom be thanks and praise for ever. Amen.

prayers.title: Confessing our fretting under affliction
prayers.opening: Thy loving-kindness is better than life; our souls shall be satisfied with that as with marrow and fatness, and then our mouths shall praise thee with joyful lips.
prayers.text: When thou hast chastised us, and we were chastised, we have been as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke; and though our own foolishness hath perverted our way, yet our heart hath fretted against the Lord; and thus in our distress we have trespassed yet more against the Lord. We have either despised the chastening of the Lord, or fainted when we have been rebuked of him; and if we faint in the day of adversity, our strength is small.
prayers.closing: Now to God the Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father, be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
prayers.author: Matthew Henry
prayers.source: arranged from A Method for Prayer, chs. 1, 2 and 7

prayers.title: For contentment and patience
prayers.opening: Thou hast appointed us a great High Priest, in whose name we may come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may find mercy and grace to help in time of need.
prayers.text: Lord, teach us whatsoever state we are in therewith to be content; let us know both how to be abased, and how to abound; every where and in all things let us be instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. And let godliness with contentment be great gain to us; and a little with the fear of the Lord and quietness, is better than great treasure and trouble therewith. Lord, grant that our conversation may be without covetousness, and we may always be content with such things as we have; still saying, The will of the Lord be done.
prayers.closing: Now unto him that is able to keep us from falling, and to present us faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, to the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, now and ever. Amen.
prayers.author: Matthew Henry
prayers.source: arranged from A Method for Prayer, chs. 1, 3 and 7

examinationQuestions: What did you complain about today, out loud or in your heart, and what did that complaint say about how you see God's wisdom and care?
What were you wanting when the discontent rose up: comfort, honor, ease, or something another person has?
Which of God's mercies to you today did you overlook or take for granted?
Has your grumbling made the load heavier for those around you, at home, at work, or in your church?
Is there a place where God has set you that you are fighting instead of serving in?
Are you more troubled by your hard circumstances or by the sin in your own heart?
fleeActions: Stop and say out loud three specific mercies God has given you today, and thank him for each one.
If a complaint is on your lips, leave it unspoken for now. Take it to God in honest prayer before you speak of it to anyone.
Do one task you have been resenting, and do it carefully, as service to Christ.
Read Philippians 4:4-13 slowly, and ask God to teach you what Paul learned.
Message a brother or sister in your church and ask them to pray that you would be content. Then ask how you can pray for them.
Write a short note of thanks to someone God has used for your good, and send it today.

afterFallReadings.text: Every man is complaining that his estate is no better, though he seldom complains that his heart is no better.
afterFallReadings.author: Thomas Watson
afterFallReadings.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 9

afterFallReadings.text: Hast thou not often been ready to conclude thyself, that it was utterly impossible that he should bear any longer with thee; that he would cast thee off, and be gracious no more; that all his forbearance was exhausted, and hell and wrath was even ready prepared for thee? and yet, above all thy expectation, he hath returned with visitations of love.
afterFallReadings.author: John Owen
afterFallReadings.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 11

afterFallReadings.text: If God be ours, whatever we want in the creature, is infinitely made up in him. Do I want bread? I have Christ the bread of life. Am I under defilement? his blood is like the trees of the sanctuary; not only for meat, but medicine.
afterFallReadings.author: Thomas Watson
afterFallReadings.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 14
